R07-D-01: The word improvisation tends to conjure an image of pure spontaneity: a musician who sits down with nothing prepared and lets whatever arrives come out. Listeners who admire improvisers often praise them in exactly these terms, as if the value of the performance lay in its having come from nowhere. Yet the image badly misdescribes what improvising musicians actually do. In the classical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, a performer exploring a raga is bound by an intricate set of expectations: which notes may be used, how the scale is approached in ascent and in descent, which phrases characterise the raga and which would make it sound like a neighbouring one. A jazz soloist working through a familiar tune is likewise held by the sequence of chords beneath the melody, by the length of each chorus and by a large shared stock of phrases that players absorb over years of listening. What these traditions share is not an absence of rules but a particular relation to them. The improviser has internalised the constraints so thoroughly that they no longer need to be consulted; they shape choices in the way grammar shapes the sentences of a fluent speaker, who does not pause to recall the rules before talking. The comparison with language is useful because it removes an apparent paradox. Nobody thinks that a conversation is unoriginal because it obeys grammar, and nobody thinks that grammar prevents people from saying things that have never been said before. On the contrary, it is the shared structure that makes a new sentence intelligible as new. This has a practical consequence for how improvisation is learned. A student who is told simply to be free usually produces something shapeless, or falls back on a handful of habits picked up by accident. Teachers in both traditions instead begin with imitation: the student copies phrases, sometimes for years, until the vocabulary becomes second nature. To an outsider this can look like the opposite of creativity. But imitation here is the means by which the constraints are absorbed, and only once they have been absorbed can the student vary them with confidence. None of this is to say that improvisation is merely the recombination of stored parts, or that the best improvisers are simply those with the largest memories. What listeners value in a great performance is often a moment at which a convention is stretched or bent in a way that still makes sense within the tradition, so that the surprise is felt as a surprise. Such moments are possible only for someone who knows exactly where the boundaries lie. Freedom in improvisation, in other words, is not freedom from form but a fluency so complete that form can be played with.
R07-D-02: Of all the performing arts, dance has the most fragile relation to its own past. A play survives in its script and a symphony in its score, so that later generations, whatever they make of these documents, at least have something to argue over. A dance, by contrast, has for most of its history existed only while it was being danced and in the memories of those who danced it. It is tempting to conclude that dance is therefore an art without a history, or one whose history is a long series of losses, and that the remedy is simply better documentation. There have been serious attempts at such documentation. Systems of dance notation have been devised that record the position of each part of the body over time, and film and video now capture performances that would once have vanished. These tools are valuable, but they have not displaced the older method of transmission, in which a dancer who has performed a role teaches it directly to a younger dancer, in a studio, by demonstration and correction. Many companies that hold detailed records of their repertoire still rely on such teaching when a work is revived, and they tend to treat the written record as an aid to memory rather than as the work itself. The reason is not mere conservatism. What passes from one body to another in the studio includes things that a notation or a recording captures poorly or not at all: the weight of a movement, the quality of attention behind it, the reasons a gesture is timed as it is. A film shows what a particular dancer did on a particular night, including her idiosyncrasies and her mistakes; it cannot say which of those features belong to the choreography and which belong to her. A teacher who has danced the role can make that distinction, or at least has a considered view about it, and passes the view on along with the steps. This method has an obvious cost. Each transmission is also an interpretation, and over several generations a dance may drift a long way from what its maker first set. Yet the drift is not simply a corruption. A dance kept alive in bodies is continually tested against the dancers who perform it, and the features that survive are usually those that dancers have found to matter. The archive of dance, on this view, is not mainly a shelf of documents but a lineage of people, and its gaps are the price of its being alive.
R07-D-03: It is often said that the phonograph and its successors simply made music available, carrying performances that had been confined to concert halls into the homes of people who would never have heard them. The claim is true as far as it goes, and the gain it describes is enormous: a listener in a small town can now hear more music in a month than a devoted concertgoer of earlier centuries could hope to hear in years. But the image of recording as a window, through which the listener observes a performance that would have happened in much the same way anyway, conceals the way recording altered both the performance and the act of listening. Consider first what repetition does. A live performance is heard once; its slips pass and are forgotten, and its moments of risk are experienced as risk. A recording is heard again and again, and on the tenth hearing a wrong note or a wavering tone is no longer a passing accident but a permanent blemish. Performers who recorded learned that what was acceptable, even exciting, in a hall could become intolerable on disc. As editing techniques improved, it became possible to assemble a single flawless performance from many takes, and the flawless performance became the standard against which the live one was measured. Listeners, in turn, came to the concert hall carrying recordings in their heads. Many now know a work first, and sometimes only, through one recorded interpretation, and they hear a live performance as a departure from it. This is a curious inversion. The recording was meant to be a copy of the performance; it has become, for many listeners, the original, and the performance its imperfect copy. Some performers have responded by playing more cautiously, aiming at the clean surface that audiences have learned to expect, at the cost of the spontaneity that once distinguished the live event. It would be wrong to treat this as a simple story of decline. Recording has also allowed listeners to compare interpretations in a way no earlier audience could, and it has preserved musical traditions that might otherwise have vanished with their last practitioners. The point is rather that recording is not neutral. A technology that lets us hear the same performance indefinitely changes what we think a performance is for, and an account of modern musical life that leaves this out has mistaken a transformation for a mere extension.
R07-D-04: Few facts about music are more familiar, or more puzzling on reflection, than the willingness of listeners to seek out music that makes them sad. People do not, on the whole, go looking for grief or disappointment in the rest of life, and they would think it odd to be offered a sorrowful afternoon as a treat. Yet slow laments, songs of loss and the darker movements of symphonies are among the most loved music in many traditions, and listeners return to them deliberately. One response dissolves the puzzle by denying its premise. On this view the listener does not really feel sad at all; she recognises sadness in the music, much as she might recognise a sorrowful expression on a carved mask, and what she enjoys is the beauty and skill with which the sadness is expressed. The view has the merit of explaining why sad music does not ruin anyone's day. But it fits poorly with what many listeners report, which is that they are moved, sometimes to tears, and not merely informed. A second response accepts that the feeling is real and explains the pleasure by the frame around it: the sadness arrives without a loss to cause it and without consequences to follow, so it can be savoured in a way that the sadness of life cannot. Both responses capture something, but both treat the emotion as a single state, present or absent, mild or intense. What music does with an emotion is closer to giving it a shape over time. A lament does not simply announce sorrow; it gathers, rises, breaks, returns to a phrase heard earlier and comes to rest. The listener who follows it is led through a version of sorrow that has a beginning, an end and a recognisable order, which is precisely what the sorrows of ordinary life usually lack. The pleasure, on this account, lies less in the feeling than in the form the feeling is given. This does not mean that sad music always pleases, or pleases everyone. Many people who are grieving find that they cannot listen to the music they loved before, at least for a time, and their experience is a useful check on any theory. A frame that keeps sadness at a safe distance should make such music easier to bear in grief, not harder. The account offered here does better: a shaped and completed sorrow may be unbearable to someone whose own sorrow has no shape yet, because the contrast is too sharp.
R07-D-05: During the twentieth century a movement grew up among performers of European music written before about 1800 that sought to recover how that music had sounded when it was new. Its adherents played on instruments built to older designs, or on surviving originals: harpsichords rather than modern pianos, gut strings rather than steel, wooden flutes without the elaborate keywork of later models. They studied treatises on performance written in the period and drew from them conclusions about tempo, ornamentation and the size of ensembles. Much of the result was a revelation. Textures that had sounded thick and heavy when played by large modern orchestras became transparent, and pieces long heard as dutiful exercises began to sound witty and alive. The difficulty lies in the word that the movement often attached to itself, authenticity. If authenticity means sounding as the music sounded to its first audiences, the goal is in one important respect unreachable. Even if every instrument and every tempo could be reconstructed exactly, the listeners could not be. An audience that has heard the music of the following two centuries hears an older piece against all of it; a dissonance that once startled may now pass unnoticed, and a small ensemble that once seemed ordinary may now sound austere and pointed. The same sounds, entering differently formed ears, do not produce the same experience. A second difficulty concerns the composers' own wishes. It is sometimes assumed that a composer who wrote for the instruments of his day would have wanted exactly those instruments, and that a performance on them is therefore more faithful to his intentions. But composers wrote for what was available, and some of them are known to have been dissatisfied with the instruments and players they had. To infer a preference from a circumstance is to confuse what a composer was given with what he would have chosen. None of this tells against the performances themselves, many of which are among the most vivid of the past century. It tells against a particular way of justifying them. The best of these performances persuade not because they are correct, in the sense of matching a lost original, but because the research behind them led performers to hear possibilities that habit had concealed. Historical evidence used in this way is less a rulebook than a provocation: a reason to try something, which must then succeed or fail as music.
R07-D-06: When collectors began, in the nineteenth century, to travel through the countryside writing down the songs of rural singers, they often approached their task as an act of rescue. The songs, they believed, were ancient and dying, and each singer they encountered was a damaged witness to an original that had once existed in a purer and more complete form. Variation between versions was evidence of decay: a verse forgotten here, a line garbled there, a tune that had wandered from its proper shape. The collector's responsibility, accordingly, was to compare the surviving fragments and reconstruct, as far as the evidence permitted, the song as it had existed before the damage began. This picture borrowed its method from the editing of ancient manuscripts, where it makes good sense. A classical text was written once by a particular author, and later copies really are more or less faithful to it. A folk song is a fundamentally different kind of object. It was never fixed in a single authoritative form; it existed only in individual performances, each of which was shaped by the singer's memory, temperament and taste, and by the particular audience and occasion. A singer who shortened a ballad for a restless crowd, or changed the name of a town to one her listeners knew, was not corrupting a text. She was doing what singers of such songs had always done, and what had made the songs worth keeping. Seen this way, variation is not the symptom of a song's decline but the very mechanism of its survival. Songs that could be adapted to unfamiliar places and new purposes travelled widely; songs that resisted such adaptation were gradually forgotten. The very versions the collectors regarded as degraded were often the ones in which a song was most alive, because they showed it being fitted to the people who still sang it. There is an irony here. By printing a single standard text, often assembled from several singers, the collectors gave the songs the fixed form they had never had, and later performers sometimes learned from the printed page instead of from other singers. It would nevertheless be unfair to dismiss the collectors' work on this account. Without their notebooks a great many songs would be irrecoverably lost, and some of them took care to record variants and the names of the singers they heard. The lesson is narrower. A record of oral music is valuable precisely to the extent that it preserves the variety which the collectors' theory taught them to regard as noise.
R07-D-07: A familiar way of thinking about Western art music divides the creative labour with reassuring neatness. The composer makes the work and records it in a score; the performer's task is to realise the score faithfully, adding as little of himself as the music allows. On this view the score is the work, or at least its complete specification, and a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains. Its attractions are considerable. It accounts for our confidence that two strikingly different performances are nevertheless performances of the same composition, and it furnishes the critic with a standard: the performer who alters the notes has made a mistake, whatever the result sounds like. The difficulty is that notation specifies far less than the view requires. A score fixes pitches and their order with considerable precision, and durations rather less, but a great deal of what listeners hear as the character of a performance is left open or indicated only roughly. A marking that asks for a loud passage does not say how loud, and the right loudness in a small room is not the right loudness in a large hall. A word indicating a lively tempo admits a range of speeds wide enough to make one performance sound urgent and another relaxed. Nothing in the marks tells the player exactly how long to linger at the high point of a phrase, or how to weigh the notes of a chord against one another. These are not trivial details that a faithful performer can safely settle at random; they are much of what makes the music sound the way it does. One response is to swing to the opposite extreme and say that the work simply is the performance, the score being no more than a set of instructions that each performer completes as she pleases. This rescues the performer's creative contribution, but at a considerable theoretical price. It cannot explain why some performances strike informed listeners as wrong-headed even when every note is in place, or why a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed has done something worse than make an unusual choice. If the score were merely a recipe to be finished at will, there would be no ground for such judgements, and yet musicians make them constantly and with considerable agreement. That agreement points to what both positions conspicuously omit. Scores are never interpreted in isolation. They are read by musicians trained in a practice: a shared and largely unwritten understanding of what the marks mean in a given style, which conventions apply, what kinds of freedom are expected and where those freedoms stop. In music of one period a trill is understood to begin on the note above; in another it begins on the main note; the score is usually silent on the point, and the practice supplies the answer. The work, on this account, is neither the marks alone nor whatever a given performance makes of them, but the marks as a practice reads them. Fidelity is owed to that combination. It may be objected that practices evolve, so that the work would apparently evolve with them, which seems absurd. But the objection establishes considerably less than it appears to. Practices do change, slowly, and the identity of a work is correspondingly less fixed than the first view supposed; that is a cost worth accepting, since it matches how musicians actually argue about performances. What does not follow is that anything goes. A practice at any moment draws lines that its members can defend, and a performer who knowingly crosses them is making a claim that must be argued for, not exercising a right.
R07-D-08: Defenders of live theatre, when pressed to explain why anyone should purchase an expensive ticket to see what could be watched more cheaply and comfortably on a screen, usually appeal to presence. The actors are there, in the same room, breathing the same air; on screen they are only images. The answer is sincere, but considered as an argument it is considerably weaker than it sounds. A great many things are physically present to us without being valuable for that reason, and a lecture delivered in person is not obviously better than the same lecture recorded. If presence were all that distinguished the stage, the case for theatre would rest on something close to a superstition about physical proximity. A more promising answer begins from what presence makes possible. A filmed performance is complete before any viewer encounters it; nothing the viewer does, however attentive or distracted, can reach back and alter it. A stage performance is still being made while the audience watches, and the audience is among the conditions under which it is made. Actors in a comedy learn to hold a line until the laughter at the previous one has crested and begun to fall, and the length of that pause differs from night to night because the laughter does. In a tense scene, a silence of a particular quality in the house tells the performers that they have the room, and they may let a moment stretch further than they would before a restless audience. These adjustments are individually small, but cumulatively they mean that a stage performance can be, in part, a response to the particular people assembled to witness it. The audience, moreover, is conscious of this reciprocity. Spectators in a theatre are aware that they can be heard and, in an intimate space, seen; they are also aware of one another, and a laugh that spreads along a row, or fails to, shapes what each person feels. The experience is less that of watching an object than of taking part, in a minor and mostly silent way, in an event whose outcome is not wholly settled. That is why a performance can fail in the theatre in a way that a film cannot: not through a flaw in its making, which a film may also have, but through a breakdown between stage and house. It may be objected that this account flatters most actual theatre, which is rarely so delicately attuned to its spectators. Many productions are drilled to such precision that they vary little from night to night, and in a large commercial house the performers can barely see past the first rows. That is true, and it calls for a qualification rather than a retraction. The responsiveness described here is a capacity of the live form, not a guarantee; a production can choose to use it or to suppress it, and one that suppresses it entirely has given up the main thing that the stage offers and the screen does not. Film, meanwhile, has resources of its own, the close-up and the edit among them, and nothing here implies that it is a lesser art. The case for live theatre, then, is not that the actors are physically near but that the performance and its audience remain capable of affecting one another. It follows, perhaps uncomfortably for some institutions, that the strongest argument for theatre is simultaneously a demand upon it. A theatre that wishes to justify its prices by appealing to liveness owes its audience a performance in which liveness actually does some work.
